turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, have a seat. It's good to see you, how have you been since we started that blood pressure tablet?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, doc, the drive from Rondebosch was a nightmare, the robot by the garage is out again. I'm alright otherwise, but this cough is what's brought me, it's been driving me up the wall.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shame, man. Tell me about the cough in your own words.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's dry, a proper tickle in the throat. I reckon it's just the tail of a cold. My grandson came up from PE full of germs, and then I got the sniffles.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did the cough itself start?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): The cold, you mean? He pitched up the weekend we had the braai, boerewors and all, and the smoke had my eyes watering. Weather was lekker that Saturday, though.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sounds like a good one. I'm still after the cough, though, when did that begin?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, sorry. Um, about three weeks, maybe four. I can't put a proper date on it, somewhere after I started the new tablet, I think.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is it every day, or does it come and go?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Every single day. Worse at night when I lie flat. A sip of water helps for a minute and then it's back, hey.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does anything come up, any phlegm?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Bone dry, nothing to spit.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you had a fever, or chills?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Not now. I was a bit fluey at the beginning, runny nose and feeling properly tired, but the nose cleared about a week ago. The tiredness has lifted too.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any shortness of breath? Pain in the chest?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I can still walk the dog up to the common. No chest pain.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any wheezing, or waking up gasping for air?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No wheeze. I do wake when the cough hits, but I'm not gasping.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): And which blood pressure tablet are you on now?

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Enalapril. My sister in Durban takes lisinopril for her pressure, she was bending my ear about it on the phone, but that's hers, not mine. Mine is enalapril, ten milligrams, one in the morning.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Every morning, or do you miss some?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly I take it. Some mornings I'm late for the school lift and I skip it, maybe two mornings a week. I'm not proud.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): And when did you actually start the enalapril?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Recently. About three weeks back, when the chemist in Claremont filled it after you phoned it through. I can't remember the exact day, shame.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else you're taking, even from the chemist?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Just that. I did buy a cough mixture at Clicks, the cheap bottle, took it for two days and stopped because it did nothing. Don't ask me the name, the label's in the bin.

[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me think this through with you. A dry cough over a few weeks can be the tail of a cold, or the enalapril, since that group of tablets is well known for a tickly cough, and reflux or asthma can do it too though I'm not hearing asthma. I'm not going to conclude today that this is the tablet. I'll keep two things open: it might be the enalapril, or it might just be that cold hanging on.

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, my sister coughed for months on the lisinopril until they swapped hers. I was blaming the grandson, though. And the load shedding, eish, I can't even boil the kettle half the time, so the honey-and-lemon thing is hit and miss.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me listen to your chest. Lungs are clear, no crackles and no wheeze. Your throat is a little red, nothing dramatic.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Is the red throat the cold still? I've been gargling salt water, my mother swore by it.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): It can linger a bit. Your blood pressure today is one hundred and forty-eight over ninety-two, and your pulse is seventy-six.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): That's higher than the machine at home, I thought I was doing lekker. The home one said something like one-thirty last week, but I don't write them down.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Home readings help if they're written down, but we'll go on today's. Any dizziness, or headaches, with the pressure?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): The dog pulled me over on Monday, nearly, he's strong for a rescue. And the garden is full of those beetles again, eating the roses.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): The beetles can wait. Dizziness or headaches, yes or no?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none of that. Head is fine, I'm not dizzy.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. How long have we been treating this blood pressure? I want to be sure I've got the story right.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): You picked it up at that check, early last year, so a bit over a year. No operations or anything, if that's next. I'm not a hospital person.

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ja, high blood pressure since early last year, and no surgery on the file, that matches. So here's what I was going to do. Keep the enalapril going, send you for a chest x-ray at the hospital, and see you back in two weeks with the picture.

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Before you book that, the cough really only kicked in a couple of days after I started those tablets. It's been dry the whole time, every day, that same tickle, worse when I lie down, though a sip of water eases it for a minute. Before that it was just sniffles, and I was so sure it was the cold.

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): That timing changes it, so scratch what I just said. We'll stop the enalapril, your blood pressure tablet, from today, and I'll start losartan fifty milligrams, one tablet every morning, for the blood pressure. No chest x-ray for now. And not two weeks, come back in four weeks so I can check the pressure on the new tablet.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Losartan. Will the cough pack up if it was the tablet? Also, Saturday's braai, can I still have a glass of wine? My brother-in-law brings the good red from Stellenbosch.

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): I still won't say the cough is definitely from the enalapril. If it is, it often settles over a few weeks after stopping, not the next day. A glass of wine is fine, I'm not cancelling the braai. If your lips or tongue swell, or you suddenly can't breathe, go to casualty the same day.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Lips swelling, got it. My sister never had that, just the cough. Four weeks is a long time if I'm still hacking at book club.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the cough is getting worse, or you become short of breath, don't wait the four weeks, come in sooner or phone the rooms. Otherwise I'll see you in four weeks.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Sharp. Do I finish the enalapril bottle or throw it?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't take another enalapril. You can drop the bottle at the chemist if you like, just don't keep using it. Start the losartan tomorrow morning.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Tomorrow, ja. And the cough mixture I binned, I'm not buying another, it was a waste of rand.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): No need for another mixture. Sip water when the tickle hits, and prop yourself up a bit at night if lying flat sets it off. That's enough on the cough for now.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Propped up, like my dad used to with his three pillows. He'll laugh if I tell him. Anyway, the parking meter is probably expired, I only put in twenty minutes.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then go rescue the car. Reception will have the losartan script and they'll book you for four weeks. Take care on that robot.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Thanks, doc. I'll try not to skip the new one on school mornings. Cheers.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. I'll see you in four weeks, and don't let that meter ticket you.

clinical_assessment.assessment: The cough might be from the enalapril or might be the tail of the cold, and it is not concluded today.
clinical_assessment.normalized_assessment: Possible enalapril-related cough versus post-viral cough
clinical_assessment.basis: Doctor keeps both the enalapril and the lingering cold open and says the cough will not be called definitely from the tablet.

spec.situation: Hypertension patient with a dry cough for weeks that they connect to 'a cold'; recently started ramipril or enalapril; they mention a relative's lisinopril. Doctor thinks aloud, changes the drug but does not give a firm diagnosis of the cough.
features: doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

bad.reason: All details supported except certainty; patient reports symptoms certainly, not uncertain.
bad.text: dry cough (category=respiratory, status=present, duration=approximately 3 to 4 weeks, frequency=every day, onset=a couple of days after starting enalapril, temporality=current, body_site=throat, aggravating_factors=lying down, relieving_factors=sipping water briefly, reported_by=patient, certainty=uncertain)

omissions.text: Enalapril adherence detail: patient misses/skips the morning dose about two mornings per week, usually on school-lift mornings.

The doctor initially planned to keep enalapril going, order a chest x-ray at the hospital, and review in two weeks, but then explicitly changed this plan after the timing history; the chest x-ray was cancelled and follow-up changed to four weeks.
The doctor assessed that reflux or asthma can also cause this kind of cough, though asthma was not suggested by the history.
Functional detail related to dyspnoea screen: patient can still walk the dog up to the common.
The patient linked the onset more specifically: the cough really only kicked in a couple of days after starting enalapril.
